doc.title: Fred Radke interviewed by Monk Rowe, Hillsdale, Michigan, November 8, 2023

chapter: From The Lancers to Harry James
title: The Lancers, Harry James as the goal, and leaving Las Vegas
summary: Playing with vocal group The Lancers at 18, his childhood vow to be James's lead trumpeter, and a bleak night in Vegas that sent him to Seattle.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Did you have it in the back of your mind that someday you might direct the Harry James Orchestra?

Well this is so — I’m playing in the East Bay in a night club, and they were booking acts like Frank Sinatra Jr., Leslie Ugg — I mean Dorothy Dandridge — my phone — and a group called The Lancers, and it was a vocal quartet. They had done a lot of T.V. They were with Kay Starr. Made some hit records. And they were headlining at Harrah’s in Tahoe, in Nevada. They were the headlining act. And in those days Bill Harrah — the lounges were very important. And they would have junkets for gamblers to go up from the Bay Area — you’d go up and get there at 8:00, you’d gamble all night, get up and leave at 8:00 in the morning to get back. And that was a big thing. So lounges, you went to work at 1:00 in the morning and worked until 5 or 6 in the morning. And Harrah’s — Bill Harrah, who was a terrific guy, he had The Lancers, he let them headliner — he had Louie Prima, he had Keely Smith, Harry James. So I said, “Ah.” The Lancers came through this nightclub and I said — and their trumpet player, which they carried, went to go with Stan Kenton as his lead player. And so they were talking about that and I thought — and I’m 18 at this time — and I said, “Hmm this is my chance to meet Harry James.” Because that’s all I want — here I’m focused on Harry James. In fact my sister the other day, on my birthday, says, “I never forgot you were about ten years old and we were in the front room with our parents and you walked in, you were practicing, you walked in with your trumpet and said, ‘I’ve decided what I’m going to do. I’m going to be Harry James’s first trumpet player’” my sister said, “and you were ten years old when you said that.” And I said, “And I’m going to do it.” My father says, “Good for you.” Right? So now this is my chance to meet Harry. Well dummy, naturally if The Lancers are the headliners at Reno, Harry’s not going to be there, he’s going to be at Tahoe. So we were never in the same venue. So now time goes on and The Lancers break up, and one guy when to go write for “Lassie” for Tom Scott’s dad, Nathan Scott. And so on, and The Lancers kind of fell apart. So I said well you know at this time I’m like 21. I’d go to Vegas and I’d put in my union card. And I really don’t know anybody in Vegas you know at that time. So one morning I was subbing on the “Steve Allen Show” or something. And I’d go out to the bar and it’s 3:00 in the morning and I’m going to get a corned beef sandwich and a beer. And this guy next to me has three hookers hanging on him drinking, slopping martinis up, and the guy next to me is having French toast with strawberries and whipped cream and I’m having a beer and a sandwich. And I look out in the casino and all this stuff going on. And I said, “God this stinks. This really is a lousy way to live.” And I thought I’ve got to get out of here. I can’t stand this. So I go over and pick up the phone and call this manager of a lady in Seattle that ran the Edmonds Yacht Club. And we had just played there with The Lancers.
